tip_title: There's an App for Your Home Inventory. It Takes About 20 Minutes.
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: There's an App for Your Home Inventory. It Takes About 20 Minutes.**

The NAIC (the National Association of Insurance Commissioners) built a free Home Inventory app specifically for this — you can scan barcodes, upload photos, and add item details room by room. It's not glamorous work, but having that record stored somewhere other than the house itself is the whole point. If a fire or major storm wipes out your belongings, the last thing you want is to reconstruct a contents claim from memory while also dealing with the aftermath. Pull it up this weekend, start with one room, and save it somewhere off-site like cloud storage or email it to yourself.

If you want to know how a solid home inventory actually connects to your personal property coverage limits, your Peachy agent can walk through that with you.

📖 [Learn more from the NAIC](https://content.naic.org/consumer/home-inventory)
summary: Covers the NAIC's free Home Inventory app as a specific tool for documenting belongings with barcode scanning and photo upload — distinct from prior tips on the video walkthrough method (April 27) and recording item values (July 10).
scoring_notes: High homeownership rates across all three audiences (78% East Cobb, 55% Perimeter, 65% Lewisville Lake) keep home inventory relevant. August has an implicit back-to-school/end-of-summer 'get your house in order' mindset hook. Prior tips covered video walkthrough method (April 27) and valuing items (July 10) — this tip introduces a specific free tool (the NAIC app) with a concrete action (start with one room this weekend), which is a distinct execution angle. NAIC is a trusted source. Repeat subject with new angle stated: prior tips covered method and valuation; this tip is about a specific free app tool that lowers the friction to actually starting.

tip_title: Back to School Means Back to the Insurance Question: What to Do About the Deductible
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: Back to School Means Back to the Insurance Question: What to Do About the Deductible**

Adding a teen to your auto policy drives the premium up — that part everyone knows. What a lot of people don't think about is the deductible side of the equation. On the physical damage coverages (collision and comprehensive), raising the deductible is one of the more direct levers for offsetting that premium jump. The tradeoff is real: a higher deductible means more out of pocket if your teen has a fender-bender, so the math only works if you've got the savings cushion to cover it. But for families where the teen is driving an older or paid-off vehicle, it's worth running the numbers before you just absorb the full rate increase.

Not sure what deductible makes sense given your situation? Your Peachy agent can walk through the actual dollar tradeoff with you.

📖 [Learn more from the NAIC](https://content.naic.org/article/consumer-insight-protect-yourself-insuring-teen-driver)
summary: Covers raising physical damage deductibles on collision and comprehensive coverages as a cost-offset strategy when adding a teen driver to an auto policy — distinct from the prior tip's focus on good student and driver ed discounts.
scoring_notes: August is prime back-to-school season — teens heading to high school or college makes this land right now. East Cobb has a strong established-family skew with teen-age kids explicitly called out; Perimeter and Lewisville Lake both have young family segments with kids. Prior July 6 tip covered good student discounts and driver ed. This tip focuses on the deductible-adjustment lever, which is a distinct and actionable angle. NAIC is a trusted source. Repeat subject with new angle stated: prior tip was about discount programs to reduce teen-driver cost; this tip is about deductible strategy as a cost-offset mechanism.
